_schema.description: Per-vendor/per-model MR scanner deliverability constants (gradient, RF, safety) with full citation provenance. Mirrors dmipy_sim biophysical_constants schema. Sections: 'scanners' (real machines, per model), 'envelopes' (declared limit points that are not a specific machine: the Pulseq presets and the Pulseq example system), 'classes' (the certificate's short names -> a scanners/envelopes key), 'aliases' (every other short name -> a key), 'safety'. Every scanner number in dmipy-sim is read from here; nothing in Python carries one.

confidence_levels.cited: value backed by a primary/authoritative source (vendor spec sheet, peer-reviewed methods paper, or IEC standard clause)
confidence_levels.widely-quoted: value is consistently reported but its primary authoritative source is unclear or coil/patient-dependent
confidence_levels.NEEDS VERIFICATION: no authoritative public source found; typically service-manual-confidential
confidence_levels.derived: value computed from a cited quantity (a slew rate from a stated rise time and amplitude); the derivation and its direction (a bound) are in context

max_amplitude.context: the WEAKEST axis across BOTH published specifications, which is what a deliverability check must use while they disagree. The regulatory filing gives X 24 / Y 23 / Z 39 mT/m and the literature gives 24.9 / 24.4 / 25.7; their minima are 23 and 24.4, so 23 is the only figure safe under either. Taking the literature's 24.4, as this leaf did, over-claims by 6 % if the filing is right -- and since the conflict is unresolved, the conservative reading is the correct one rather than the cautious one. Per-axis values and the conflict itself are in per_axis_amplitude_fda and per_axis_amplitude_literature; which physical direction each axis names is not public.
max_amplitude.location: Comparison of Technological Characteristics, Gradient: Strength (weakest axis)

max_slew_rate.context: the WEAKEST axis; per axis X / Y / Z = 23 / 22 / 67 T/m/s. No PNS derating applies at these slews

per_axis_amplitude_fda.context: the regulatory filing's per-axis gradient strength, as vendor axes X / Y / Z. WHICH PHYSICAL DIRECTION EACH LABEL NAMES IS NOT PUBLIC, and the evidence conflicts. Three things point to the vendor's Z being the B0-parallel (vertical, anterior-posterior) axis: it is the outlier in both hardware generations' FDA tables, strong and slow, which is the signature of the plate-normal winding in a bi-planar set. Against it, Hyperfine's own hysteresis patent US 2024/0142556 A1 discusses MEASURED data and says 'the B0 field is oriented along the y-axis... the y-gradient coil induces magnetization along the y-axis' -- the only primary document binding a Hyperfine coil label to the field direction, and it says Y. A third source (the Leiden data descriptor) writes 'the AP direction is considered the z-axis', but the same document labels its 3 T scanner differently, so it is declaring the universal z-is-B0 convention rather than reporting vendor labels. One measurement narrows it: across the NIST database the per-axis echo times are identical for every subject and ordered image-x 83.600 < image-y 83.640 < image-z 84.110 ms, so the S/I axis is the most expensive and the vendor's outlier is probably not S/I -- which leaves A/P or R/L. Not decisive: 0.5 ms in 84 also carries slice selection and readout.
per_axis_amplitude_fda.location: Comparison of Technological Characteristics, Gradient: Strength

per_axis_amplitude_literature.context: the same three axes as reported in the peer-reviewed literature, and IRRECONCILABLE with the filing on the third: 25.7 against 39 mT/m, a factor 1.52. A full-text search of the literature for this machine and '39 mT/m' returns nothing. The conflict is unresolved and is recorded rather than adjudicated. The companion slew disagreement (21 against 67 T/m/s on the third axis) does NOT affect concomitant fields, which go as G^2/B0 and never see a slew rate. concomitant_alpha.context: the gradient coils' symmetry parameter in the concomitant-field expansion. It is NOT a universal constant, and treating it as one is the standard silent assumption: alpha = 1/2 follows from cylindrical symmetry and holds for the fingerprint coils of a conventional bore magnet, but a Halbach array gives alpha = 0, which produces a SINGLE cross-term of double amplitude instead of the conventional pair and makes the concomitant field grow transversally rather than axially. For this machine it is 1/2, and by an argument rather than by default: de Vos et al. state the value 'also holds for parallel plate gradient coils in an open C- or H-shaped magnet', and the Swoop is an H-shaped magnet with bi-planar gradient coils. Nobody has published concomitant fields for this machine or for any bi-planar 64 mT magnet, so this is an inference from a class statement. The companion parameter beta is taken as zero, which is the symmetric-coil case; an ASYMMETRIC gradient coil adds zeroth- and first-order concomitant terms that do not vanish at isocentre MEASURED FROM GEOMETRY (dmipy-sim#364 tier 1): a Biot-Savart bi-planar pair gives alpha = 0.5000 for SQUARE plates at any gap, since square plates are four-fold symmetric about B0 and the two transverse directions are then equivalent. Both of the published values come out of that one family, so de Vos's 1/2 and 0 are one geometry at two parameter points rather than two facts. BUT THE CONTROLLING PARAMETER IS THE PAIR (width/gap, length/gap), NOT the plate aspect ratio: at a fixed aspect ratio of three, alpha runs 0.02 to 0.43 as the gap grows, because a pair whose gap dwarfs both plate dimensions degenerates to an axially symmetric dipole pair; alpha approaches 0 only when one plate dimension greatly exceeds the gap. So the inference for this machine needs BOTH ratios and this catalogue records neither, which makes 1/2 less constrained than it reads rather than more. It is not a safe default: at 64 mT with 23 mT/m over TE 110 ms, alpha = 1/2 against alpha = 0 differs by 3.85x in the concomitant field 10 cm along x and by hundreds of radians of phase, and at alpha = 0 the field VANISHES along z while growing along x, which independently reproduces de Vos's description of a single cross-term growing transversally rather than axially. One further caution the measurement exposed: alpha = 1/2 does NOT by itself mean a symmetric coil, since an asymmetric one read at 45 degrees to its own principal axes reads 1/2 as well while the concomitant field the alpha model predicts is wrong by orders of magnitude there.
concomitant_alpha.location: Theory, the symmetry parameter for parallel-plate gradient coils

b0_homogeneity.context: over a 16 cm DSV; the magnet is asymmetric in RL

background_gradient.context: the magnet's own field gradient at 8 cm from isocentre, up to 7 % of the diffusion gradient; it encodes diffusion alongside the pulsed gradient and the paper corrects ADC errors of up to 16.1 % with the b = 0 image

b0_validity_radius.context: how far from isocentre b0_quadratic is anchored: the radius the cited gradient was measured at. The law is an extrapolation beyond this and a consumer refuses rather than extrapolating. The law is now a solid-harmonic expansion truncated at l=3, so beyond this radius it is doubly an extrapolation: in radius, and in the orders that were never constrained

b0_asymmetry_axis.context: the patient-frame direction the odd harmonic is odd along: the magnet is 'asymmetric in the RL-direction' because a single yoke sits on one side. The SIGN is a convention -- the source does not say which side is high -- and a study that cares about the direction must check it. This axis and b0_axis together fix the frame the harmonics are written in, so the law needs no third convention

b0_harmonic_Z2.context: the coefficient of the standard shim term Z2 = 2 zeta^2 - xi^2 - eta^2, in the real solid-harmonic basis and nomenclature magnet builders and shim hardware use (Romeo & Hoult 1984) -- the same Z2 a console labels. Coordinates are the magnet's own: zeta along B0, xi along the declared asymmetry axis. THIS IS ONE ADMISSIBLE LAW, NOT THE LAW. Two published figures against fifteen solid-harmonic coefficients of order 2 to 4 is an underdetermined fit, and the degeneracy has been measured rather than assumed: 400 laws sampled, each harmonic and each reproducing BOTH figures exactly, disagree about the background gradient's DIRECTION by a median 71 degrees (90th percentile 134) and about its magnitude at a given point by 36 per cent. What they agree on is the scale -- the steepest gradient in the DSV is 1.400 mT/m in every one by construction, and the shell-average magnitude varies only 18 per cent. So a quantity driven by the WORST gradient is determined and one driven by the gradient's direction or its value at a particular place is not. See examples/rph/swoop_field_law_degeneracy.py.
b0_harmonic_Z2.location: solved against the Methods' DSV homogeneity and the Appendix's background gradient

b0_harmonic_Z2X.context: the coefficient of the standard shim term Z2X = xi(4 zeta^2 - xi^2 - eta^2), odd in xi and therefore this magnet's R/L asymmetry. WHY ORDER THREE. The published homogeneity is a POST-LINEAR-SHIM residual -- the source says the magnet was 'B0 shimmed, using linear (gradient) B0 shimming' -- so the l=1 content is nulled and cannot be fitted to it. Order three is then forced by the two figures together. Both constraints scale with the coefficients, so what they pin is the scale-invariant ratio max|grad| / peak-to-peak x R, and the cited 1.4 mT/m at 1100 ppm over a 16 cm DSV requires 1.591. Maximising that ratio over ALL MIXTURES of a given order (not over pure terms, which is a weaker bound and reaches only 1.364 and 1.572 respectively) gives 1.364 through l=2 and 1.971 through l=3. So l<=2 cannot produce this magnet and l=3 can: order three is an inference about the hardware, not a modelling choice. THIS IS ONE ADMISSIBLE LAW, NOT THE LAW. b0_harmonic_Z2X.location: Methods, scanner description ('asymmetric in RL'); magnitude solved with b0_harmonic_Z2

b0_direction_spread_deg.context: the median angle by which admissible field laws disagree about the background gradient's DIRECTION at a point on the 7.55 cm shell; the 90th percentile is 134 degrees. Measured over 400 sampled laws, each harmonic and each reproducing both published figures exactly. This is not an error bar on a measurement -- nobody measured the direction -- it is the width of what two scalars leave open. Any quantity that depends on where the background gradient POINTS carries it; one that depends only on how steep the field gets does not

b0_gradient_point_spread.context: the relative spread (sd/mean) of the background gradient's MAGNITUDE at a fixed point, across the same 400 admissible laws. For contrast the shell-AVERAGE magnitude varies only 18 per cent and the volume-steepest is identical in all of them at 1.400 mT/m, being one of the two fitted figures. So the scale of this field is determined and its shape is not

hyperfine_swoop_64mT.notes: A permanent magnet's field follows its temperature, and this one is passively cooled with no temperature control over its cleared 15-30 degC range (510(k)). The measured coefficient is -1400 Hz/K = -514 ppm/K (ljungberg2025_unity, 244 scans at 17 sites) -- about HALF the bulk NdFeB figure, and what the machine is actually made of is not public. Two things keep that from reaching the data: the pre-scan calibration removes the between-session ambient term entirely, and the protocol re-centres f0 after every two DWIs (every volume, for royer2026_tract_64mT), attributing the within-scan drift to GRADIENT heating. (The 50 mT Halbach is the other way round -- there the gradients heat the magnet negligibly and the body is the source.) The gradients are passively cooled, which caps protocols near an hour. Its diffusion sequence is a non-CPMG SPLICE split-echo train (ohalloran2022_dwi_64mt).

b1_axial_falloff.context: the coefficient a of kappa_B1 = 1 - a z^2 about the coil's centre, z along the bore (superior-inferior). Derived from a measured B1+ map: 'little appreciable inhomogeneity in the transverse plane' and '15%-20% variation in the superior-inferior direction' over a 144 mm spherical phantom, so the fall-off is taken at the midpoint 17.5 % across the sphere's 72 mm half-extent. It is FLAT transversally, which is why this has no radial term -- the anisotropy is the citation's, not a simplification. A 180 degree pulse therefore delivers 148 degrees at the edge of that sphere. The transverse behaviour is NOT a second measurement and carries no second leaf: at 2.7 MHz the coil bore is quasi-static, so the paraxial expansion of the field is B(s) - (rho^2/4) B''(s) and asserting the axial fall-off DETERMINES a transverse rise. Laplace pins the SUM of the two transverse curvatures at 2a and an azimuthally symmetric coil splits it equally, giving rho^2/2. This coil is oblong (205 x 240 mm), so its true split is unequal and unpublished -- which is also why the source can report 'little appreciable inhomogeneity in the transverse plane' without contradicting the physics: it constrains one direction where the constraint is on the pair. An equal split is the symmetric choice, not a measured one
b1_axial_falloff.location: Results, Figure 3A-B (actual flip-angle imaging, 144 mm spherical phantom)

b1_calibration_offset.context: a SYSTEMATIC transmit scale, not a spatial one: 'the expected signal null at 180 degrees was consistently offset to 190 degrees, perhaps due to B1 errors', which is a scale of 190/180. It applies everywhere including isocentre, so it is separate from b1_axial_falloff and multiplies it. The same source reports a spread of about +/- 20 degrees around 300, i.e. +/- 6.7 %
b1_calibration_offset.location: Discussion, flip-angle sweep (1-420 degrees) on hardware v1.7

b1_load_independent.context: why a transmit profile is a property of the MACHINE at this field and may live in a scanner catalogue at all. At 2.7 MHz the RF wavelength in tissue is metres, so dielectric and standing-wave effects vanish: simulation across 47-100 mT in a 40-tissue head model finds 'only a 3% spatial variation between the maps obtained at 47 mT and 100 mT' while tissue permittivity changes by about 30 %. This value is that 3 %. The same claim must NOT be extended to 3 T or 7 T, where the profile is substantially the subject's
b1_load_independent.location: Results, normalized difference maps across 47/63.5/75/100 mT

f0_temperature_slope.context: how far the centre frequency moves per kelvin of ambient temperature, as PUBLISHED: a slope of -0.0014 MHz/degC from a linear mixed-effects regression of the DICOM centre frequency on phantom temperature over 244 scans at 17 sites, with site as a random effect (the sites differ in baseline frequency but not in slope). This is the only measured temperature coefficient of THIS machine. Its scope is narrow and matters: it is an AMBIENT sensitivity BETWEEN sessions over 18-24.5 degC, not a within-scan drift rate, and the phantom thermometer was discrete vials about a kelvin apart and censored at 24.5 degC, so the slope is more likely biased toward zero than away from it

b0_temperature_coefficient.context: the same measured slope as a fraction of B0: -1400 Hz / 2.725 MHz = -514 ppm/K. Divided out here rather than in a consumer, because the published figure is in hertz and the field law is a fraction. Worth knowing that this is about HALF the bulk NdFeB remanence coefficient (-0.09 to -0.12 %/K, quoted as ~-0.1 %/K by cooley2021_portable and measured as 2.5 kHz/degC at 50 mT by oreilly2021_halbach): the magnet is not all permanent-magnet material -- a steel yoke captures part of the flux and its permeability has a different, smaller temperature dependence. So the materials constant OVERSTATES this machine by a factor of two, and the measured figure is the one to use. Note also that no public document states what the Swoop's magnet is MADE of; the FDA filings and the specification sheet say only 'permanent magnet', and NdFeB appears in Hyperfine's patent US11215685B2 only as an example alongside SmCo, which is explicitly offered as the lower-drift alternative. At 514 ppm/K it takes about 2.1 K to equal this magnet's whole 1100 ppm spatial inhomogeneity
b0_temperature_coefficient.location: derived from the Results slope at f0 = gamma_bar x 0.064 T = 2.7249 MHz

operating_temperature_span.context: the width of the ambient range the scanner is cleared for, 15-30 degC, over which it has NO temperature control and no humidity control -- the 510(k) comparison table says so in as many words, alongside 'warm up time < 3 minutes' and no helium. The span matters because the magnet is uncontrolled across it: at the measured 514 ppm/K the two ends of the cleared range are 7700 ppm apart, 21 kHz, which is why the centre frequency is a calibration and never an assumption. The between-session ambient spread is in practice the LARGEST thermal term -- the UNITY sites span 18 to over 24.5 degC and many sit in unregulated rooms -- and it is entirely removed by the pre-scan calibration, which is why it never reaches the data
operating_temperature_span.location: technological characteristics comparison table, Operation Temperature / Temperature Control

f0_recentering_interval.context: how long the field is left to drift before the centre frequency is re-set: the Swoop's diffusion protocol re-centres f0 after every TWO DWIs following a short calibration scan, 'to account for B0 drift induced by gradient heating'. Two volumes of 212 shots at TR 800 ms is 339 s. This is what makes drift a small effect rather than a large one -- the accumulated offset is discarded and only what accrues within the interval reaches the data. It is an UPPER bound on current practice: a second group re-centres between every diffusion volume (royer2026_tract_64mT), which halves it. NO within-scan drift RATE is published for this machine. The nearest analogues are 50 mT Halbach systems at 800-1300 Hz/h, which is 0.32-0.52 K/h at their own 2.5 kHz/K; carried over at the Swoop's measured 1400 Hz/K that is 450-730 Hz/h, so 42-69 Hz within this interval. That is an estimate from another magnet's warming rate, not a measurement of this one
f0_recentering_interval.location: Methods, diffusion acquisition; the shot count and TR from ohalloran2022_dwi_64mt

b0_axis.context: the patient's ANTERIOR direction. Hyperfine's own patent states the bi-planar arrangement puts B0 'along a vertical axis', and that the RF coil therefore has 'a principal axis aligned with a horizontal axis orthogonal to the vertical axis'. For a supine patient vertical is anterior-posterior, so B0 runs across the patient rather than along them -- the opposite of every cylindrical magnet. This is the single fact that makes a magnet frame necessary at all: on a bore scanner B0, the bore and the coil axis coincide and nothing distinguishes them. The SIGN is a convention; no source says which way the field points, and nothing here depends on it
b0_axis.location: specification, bi-planar B0 magnet and RF coil orientation

b1_axis.context: the patient's head-foot direction: the transmit coil's principal axis, perpendicular to B0 as a solenoid's must be. The 510(k) designates the head coil 'Linear Volume' with a single transmit channel, which is consistent -- a quadrature birdcage CANNOT be used in this geometry, so the coil has one axis and the falloff law has something to be a function of
b1_axis.location: specification, RF coil principal axis; coil class from FDA K221923

d_scale_x_dx.context: how the gradient actually delivered along x mis-scales per metre of LEFT-RIGHT displacement: the xx element of the gradient-nonlinearity tensor L, whose derivative with respect to x this is. Standard error 0.0539 /m over 10 participants (not significant). Measured, not vendor-published: regressed from the NIST dual-field database, where each participant's diffusivity is fitted separately along x, y and z. Encoding along u and fitting against the NOMINAL b measures ADC_u = (L u)^T D (L u), so a fractional gradient error appears DOUBLED in the diffusivity and the slope is halved to get this. TWO LIMITS, both structural. (1) Only the TRACELESS part is observable: normalising each axis by the trace is what removes the unknown true diffusivity, and it forces the three coefficients to sum to zero, so a common mode -- all three axes mis-scaled together -- is invisible here and is NOT included. (2) The x dependence is the only one that can be claimed: every per-axis diffusivity is invariant under a left-right mirror, so mirror-symmetric anatomy cannot make a linear term in x and any such term is instrumental, while a trend in y or z would be indistinguishable from anatomy. Attributing it to gradient AMPLITUDE rather than to a rotation of the encoding frame is an inference: a rotation enters at second order and would need an implausible 0.3 rad/m, whereas an amplitude error enters at first order and needs 0.45 %/cm. Eddy currents and any vendor distortion correction already in the product reconstruction are NOT excluded
d_scale_x_dx.location: derived from participants 00-09, per-axis diffusivity regressed on left-right position

gradient_completion.context: THE ONE MEMBER OF THIS TENSOR'S FREEDOM THAT IS EXPOSED -- not the only one that exists. The NIST regression measures the DIAGONAL of the gradient-nonlinearity tensor, dL_jj/dx, and nothing else. Harmonicity and L(0) = I do not then determine the rest: for EACH of the three coils the admissible potentials form a four-parameter affine family in this basis (six in the full order-four space), since any two-dimensional harmonic in the other two coordinates with zero gradient at the origin may be added without touching the measured diagonal. What ships is the MINIMUM-NORM member, which is provably unique (every free direction is a distinct solid harmonic and so is orthogonal to the particular solution, making zero the unique minimiser of added field energy), is the lowest-order member, and is the only one keeping each coil's reflection parity -- B_z odd in the axis it encodes, the ideal Golay and Maxwell winding symmetry. Under that parity assumption the family collapses to a point; the assumption is a modelling choice and is NOT in the data, and note the model already asserts one ideal parity is broken, since a non-zero a_j is a breach of parity in x. THE UNSTATED CHOICE IS THE LARGER ONE: an admissible alternative breaking the y coil's parity by as much as the measured effect moves L by the whole modelled nonlinearity and a b value by a few per cent, and the tier-0 admissibility gate cannot distinguish it. This leaf's own number is the share of the x coil's curvature taken from y; 1/2 is the least-committed split and is that sub-family's minimum-norm point. It is cheap -- over the validity radius the whole lam family spans 3.5 per cent of the nonlinearity and 0.001 per cent of a b value, because a_x is the smallest of the three coefficients at 7 per cent of the largest -- but it is one line inside the four-dimensional freedom above, not a different kind of thing. A DIAGONAL L is not an option at any lam: it would make each coil's B_z depend on its own axis alone, and Laplace then forces that dependence to be linear, so a diagonal L is the identity or it is not a field at all.
gradient_completion.location: not a location in the data: the share is fixed by convention, since the measurement constrains only the diagonal and the x coil's harmonic completion is one-parameter

averaging_window_volume_coil.context: SAR is averaged over any 6-minute period for whole-body, partial-body and head (volume transmit coils)

averaging_window_local.context: short-term/local SAR averaging; short-term SAR over any 10 s shall not exceed 2x the stated 6-min averaged limit

whole_body_first_level.context: First-Level Controlled Operating Mode, whole-body average

head_normal.context: Normal Operating Mode, head average (volume coil); same 3.2 limit applies in First-Level mode for head

head_first_level.context: First-Level Controlled Operating Mode, head average (volume coil)

local_head_normal.context: Normal Operating Mode, local SAR in head (local transmit coil), 10 g averaging

local_head_first_level.context: First-Level Controlled Operating Mode, local SAR in head (local transmit coil)

local_trunk_normal.context: Normal Operating Mode, local SAR in trunk

local_trunk_first_level.context: First-Level Controlled Operating Mode, local SAR in trunk

local_extremities_normal.context: Normal Operating Mode, local SAR in extremities

local_extremities_first_level.context: First-Level Controlled Operating Mode, local SAR in extremities

partial_body_normal.context: Partial-body scales with exposed mass ratio r: SAR_limit = (10 - 8*r) W/kg in Normal mode

partial_body_first_level.context: Partial-body: SAR_limit = (10 - 6*r) W/kg in First-Level Controlled mode

second_level_controlled.context: Second-Level Controlled mode: above First-Level limits, requires ethics/IRB approval; no fixed IEC numeric ceiling

temperature_derating.context: all SAR limits assume ambient <= 25 degC; derate by ~0.25 W/kg for each degC above 25 (see Fig 201.103, Table 201.104)

definition.context: B1+rms is the RMS of the B1+ field over a defined averaging period (commonly stated as 10 s); IEC 60601-2-33 mandates that B1+rms be a user-selectable/displayed output (MR Equipment Output Conditioning, MROC) so it can be matched to MR-Conditional implant labeling. It is patient-mass-independent. There is NO single fixed numeric IEC ceiling for B1+rms; the limit is set by the implant's MR-Conditional label.
definition.location: Clause 201.12.4.103 / FPO output display requirements; see also mriquestions B1+rms

basis.context: Gradient output (dB/dt) is limited so as not to exceed the peripheral-nerve-stimulation (PNS) threshold. IEC 60601-2-33 expresses the limit via the rheobase/chronaxie stimulation model: Normal mode <= 80% of mean PNS threshold; First-Level <= 100% of mean PNS threshold; cardiac stimulation must always be avoided (Fig 201.102).

pns_threshold_model.context: Annex AA gives the strength-duration (rheobase/chronaxie) PNS threshold formulation and the dB/dt response-value convolution model (Figs AA.3-AA.7).

architecture.context: SAFE = Stimulation Approximation by Filtering and Evaluation. The gradient G(t) is differentiated (dG/dt), then split into >=2 (optionally 3) parallel low-pass filter branches with time constants tau1, tau2 (tau3 optional), each rectified, weighted by scale factors a1,a2,a3 and summed to form Stim(t); stimulation predicted if Stim(t) > Stim_lim. Empirical, vendor-implemented as a dB/dt watchdog.

weight_constraint.context: the weighting scale factors are normalized: a1 + a2 + a3 = 1.0

time_constant_range.context: filter time constants stated to lie in the ~5..15 ms range in the abstract; the specific per-filter tau1/tau2/tau3 values and per-coil scale factors a1/a2/a3 are NOT published (vendor-calibrated per gradient coil).
time_constant_range.location: Hebrank & Gebhardt 2000, Results ('5..15 ms with a1+a2+a3 = 1.0')

coefficients.context: Exact SAFE tau and a coefficients per gradient coil are vendor-confidential; only the architecture and normalization are published.

example_coefficients.context: The REPRESENTATIVE example gradient system's SAFE coefficients (per axis: three RC time constants, their normalised weights a1+a2+a3 = 1, the stimulation limit and the gradient scale), as shipped with safe_pns_prediction and pypulseq. NOT any specific scanner's calibration -- those are vendor-confidential (see 'coefficients'). The SAFE solver lives in dmipy-design; this is the data it reads.
example_coefficients.location: example hardware file in the repository

max_amplitude.context: the PULSEQ_SYSTEMS 'clinical_typical' preset: a nominal clinical system, not a machine

the PULSEQ_SYSTEMS 'preclinical_bruker' preset: a nominal preclinical system, not a machine (the cited Bruker systems are bruker_bga_9s, bruker_bga_12s_hp, bruker_bga_6s, bruker_micro2_5, bruker_micro5)

rf_dead_time.context: RF dead time of the example system used by Pulseq exporters so check_timing is meaningful; no vendor spec sheet publishes one (the Prisma leaf is NEEDS VERIFICATION for that reason). Was hard-coded in dmipy-design pulseq_export._DEAD.

adc_dead_time.context: example-system ADC dead time, as rf_dead_time
